book.title: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
book.lead: Pulmonary rehabilitation is one of the most effective treatments in all of medicine for breathless patients.

blocks.text: COPD is a common, preventable lung disease with persistent airflow limitation and respiratory symptoms, usually caused by smoking, biomass fuel smoke or occupational exposure. It includes emphysema (destruction of alveoli and loss of elastic recoil) and chronic bronchitis (chronic productive cough). Airways narrow and collapse during expiration, trapping air. Lungs become hyperinflated, flattening the diaphragm and making breathing inefficient. The resulting breathlessness leads to inactivity, deconditioning, and more breathlessness: the **dyspnoea spiral**.
Diagnosis is confirmed by spirometry: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.70 [Ref – to verify GOLD current report].

items: Progressive breathlessness on exertion, chronic cough, sputum, wheeze.
Barrel chest, use of accessory muscles, pursed-lip breathing, tripod posture.
Exacerbations: acute worsening of breathlessness, sputum volume or purulence.
Weight loss and muscle wasting in advanced disease; ankle oedema with cor pulmonale.

blocks.text: Vital signs and SpO2 at rest; observation; auscultation; chest expansion; peripheral oedema; body mass index; quadriceps strength; exercise test (6MWT or shuttle walk) with SpO2 monitoring; CAT score (COPD Assessment Test) and mMRC.

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Acute severe breathlessness, unable to speak, confusion, drowsiness
Emergency team; controlled oxygen to prescribed target
SpO2 persistently below target during exercise despite rest

blocks.label: STOP AND THINK
body: Giving high-flow oxygen to a patient with hypercapnic COPD can worsen CO2 retention. Follow the prescribed target, often 88 to 92% [Ref – to verify].

steps: **Exacerbation in hospital:** breathing control, positioning, airway clearance if sputum is a problem, early mobilisation, consider NIV support with the team.
**Stable:** refer to (or deliver) pulmonary rehabilitation; start after an exacerbation as soon as the patient is able, ideally within weeks [Ref – to verify].
**Desaturation on exercise?** Assess need for supplemental oxygen during training.

sections.title: I. Breathing techniques and airway clearance

rows: Relaxed shoulders, gentle tidal breathing through the nose, using the lower chest
Breathe in through the nose, out slowly through lips shaped as if whistling, exhale about twice as long as inhale
Forward lean sitting with forearms on thighs or a table; forward lean standing against a wall
Breathing control, then 3 to 4 deep breaths with a hold, then breathing control, then huffs (medium then short), repeat
Positive expiratory pressure (PEP) or oscillating PEP devices
10 to 15 breaths through the device, then huffs
"Blow as you go": exhale during the effort

sections.title: J. Pulmonary rehabilitation (example program, not universal)

rows: 3 to 5 days a week; start about 60 to 80% of 6MWT walking speed, or at Borg dyspnoea 3 to 4; 20 to 30 min total, intervals allowed
Borg falls below 3 at the same workload
Patients too breathless for continuous work
Major muscle groups, especially quadriceps; 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 reps at a load that is moderately hard
Unsupported arm exercises (arm activities are very breathless for COPD patients)
Consider if inspiratory muscles are weak [Ref – to verify]
Self-management, medication and inhaler technique, exacerbation action plan, energy conservation, smoking cessation

blocks.text: Program length is typically 6 to 12 weeks, at least twice weekly supervised [Ref – to verify]. Maintenance exercise afterwards is essential.

Supplemental oxygen during exercise for those who desaturate, as prescribed. Non-invasive ventilation during training only in specialist settings. Neuromuscular electrical stimulation for very weak, deconditioned patients who cannot exercise [Ref – to verify].

blocks.label: CLINICAL CASE
body: A 66-year-old ex-smoker (45 pack-years) with COPD, mMRC 3, walks 260 m in 6MWT with SpO2 falling from 93% to 85% on room air, Borg 6. Two admissions this year. Goal: walk to the market.

items: **Can he start pulmonary rehabilitation?** Yes, after medical review of oxygen needs during exercise because he desaturates.
**What starting intensity would you choose?** Walking at about 60 to 80% of his 6MWT speed or at Borg 3 to 4, with intervals and supplemental oxygen as prescribed.
**Why include arm training?** Unsupported arm activities cause disproportionate breathlessness.
**What breathing technique helps him on stairs?** Pursed-lip breathing and "blow as you go" pacing.
**What does an mMRC of 3 mean?** He stops for breath after about 100 metres or a few minutes on level ground.
Initial approach: pulmonary rehabilitation with education.
Priority: exercise capacity, breathlessness management, self-management.
Techniques: breathing control, pursed-lip breathing, positions of ease, ACBT if sputum.
Avoid: uncontrolled high-flow oxygen in hypercapnic patients; bed rest.
Measure: 6MWT, CAT, mMRC.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Explain the dyspnoea spiral and hyperinflation.
Teach breathing control, pursed-lip breathing and ACBT.
Prescribe and progress a pulmonary rehabilitation program.
Recognise exacerbation and hypercapnic risk.
